<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Appendix B <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Proofs &amp; Comments</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">B.13</span> Reparametrization invariance of the length (§<a class="dg-xref" href="../metric/length-geodesics.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Length_Geodesics">7.2</a>)</h1></header>
<p>Let <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, g)\)</span> be a Riemannian metric manifold, <span class="math inline">\(\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{M}\)</span> a smooth curve with speed <span class="math inline">\(s_\gamma\)</span>, and <span class="math inline">\(a &lt; b\)</span>. Recall that <span class="math inline">\(L_{[a,b]}[\gamma] \coloneqq \int_a^b s_\gamma(\lambda) \, d\lambda\)</span>, where the integral exists because <span class="math inline">\(s_\gamma\)</span>, the square root of a continuous non-negative function, is continuous on <span class="math inline">\([a,b]\)</span>.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Reparametrizations.</strong> A <strong>reparametrization</strong> is a diffeomorphism <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ} : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\)</span>, i.e. a smooth bijection with smooth inverse. Equivalently, <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}\)</span> is a smooth bijection with <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}'(\tilde{\lambda}) \neq 0\)</span> for all <span class="math inline">\(\tilde{\lambda} \in \mathbb{R}\)</span>:</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>If <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}^{-1}\)</span> is differentiable, applying the chain rule to <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}^{-1} \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ} = \mathrm{id}_\mathbb{R}\)</span> gives <span class="math inline">\((\textrm{\runic ᚱ}^{-1})'\big( \textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{\lambda}) \big) \cdot \textrm{\runic ᚱ}'(\tilde{\lambda}) = 1\)</span>, so <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}'(\tilde{\lambda}) \neq 0\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p>Conversely, if <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}'(\tilde{\lambda}) \neq 0\)</span> everywhere, the inverse function theorem makes <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}^{-1}\)</span> smooth, with derivative <span class="math inline">\((\textrm{\runic ᚱ}^{-1})'(\lambda) = 1 / \textrm{\runic ᚱ}'\big( \textrm{\runic ᚱ}^{-1}(\lambda) \big)\)</span>.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>A smooth bijection alone does not suffice: <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{\lambda}) = \tilde{\lambda}^3\)</span> is one, but <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}'(0) = 0\)</span> and its inverse, <span class="math inline">\(\lambda \mapsto \lambda^{1/3}\)</span>, is not differentiable at <span class="math inline">\(0\)</span>. Since <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}'\)</span> is continuous and never vanishes, it has a constant sign: <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}\)</span> is either <strong>orientation preserving</strong> (<span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}' &gt; 0\)</span>) or <strong>orientation reversing</strong> (<span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}' &lt; 0\)</span>). In both cases <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}^{-1}([a,b])\)</span> is a closed interval <span class="math inline">\([\tilde{a}, \tilde{b}]\)</span>, with <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{a}) = a\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{b}) = b\)</span> in the first case and <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{a}) = b\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{b}) = a\)</span> in the second.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Statement.</strong> For every reparametrization <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}\)</span>, the reparametrized curve <span class="math inline">\(\delta \coloneqq \gamma \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}\)</span>, which traces the same path as <span class="math inline">\(\gamma\)</span>, satisfies <span class="math display">\[
    L_{[\tilde{a}, \tilde{b}]}[\delta] = L_{[a,b]}[\gamma],
    \qquad [\tilde{a}, \tilde{b}] \coloneqq \textrm{\runic ᚱ}^{-1}\big( [a,b] \big).
\]</span></p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Proof.</strong></p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p><em>Velocities.</em> At every <span class="math inline">\(\tilde{\lambda} \in \mathbb{R}\)</span>, both curves pass through the same point, <span class="math inline">\(\delta(\tilde{\lambda}) = \gamma\big( \textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{\lambda}) \big)\)</span>, so their velocities live in the same tangent space. For every <span class="math inline">\(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)</span>, the ordinary chain rule for the composition of the real functions <span class="math inline">\(f \circ \gamma\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}\)</span> gives  <span class="math display">\[
            v_{\delta(\tilde{\lambda})}(f)
            = \big( (f \circ \gamma) \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ} \big)'(\tilde{\lambda})
            = (f \circ \gamma)'\big( \textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{\lambda}) \big) \cdot \textrm{\runic ᚱ}'(\tilde{\lambda})
            = \textrm{\runic ᚱ}'(\tilde{\lambda}) \cdot v_{\gamma, \gamma(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{\lambda}))}(f).
        \]</span>  Since this holds for every <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span>, the two velocities are proportional,  <span class="math display">\[
            v_{\delta(\tilde{\lambda})} = \textrm{\runic ᚱ}'(\tilde{\lambda}) \, v_{\gamma, \gamma(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{\lambda}))} \in T_{\delta(\tilde{\lambda})}\mathcal{M}.
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p><em>Speeds.</em> By the bilinearity of <span class="math inline">\(g_{\delta(\tilde{\lambda})}\)</span>,  <span class="math display">\[
            s_\delta(\tilde{\lambda})
            = \sqrt{ g_{\delta(\tilde{\lambda})}\big( v_{\delta(\tilde{\lambda})}, v_{\delta(\tilde{\lambda})} \big) }
            = \sqrt{ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}'(\tilde{\lambda})^2 \; g_{\gamma(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{\lambda}))}\big( v_{\gamma, \gamma(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{\lambda}))}, v_{\gamma, \gamma(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{\lambda}))} \big) }
            = |\textrm{\runic ᚱ}'(\tilde{\lambda})| \; s_\gamma\big( \textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{\lambda}) \big).
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p><em>Lengths.</em> Substituting <span class="math inline">\(\lambda = \textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{\lambda})\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(d\lambda = \textrm{\runic ᚱ}'(\tilde{\lambda}) \, d\tilde{\lambda}\)</span>, in the orientation preserving case, <span class="math inline">\(|\textrm{\runic ᚱ}'| = \textrm{\runic ᚱ}'\)</span>,  <span class="math display">\[
            L_{[\tilde{a}, \tilde{b}]}[\delta]
            = \int_{\tilde{a}}^{\tilde{b}} s_\gamma\big( \textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{\lambda}) \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᚱ}'(\tilde{\lambda}) \, d\tilde{\lambda}
            = \int_{\textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{a})}^{\textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{b})} s_\gamma(\lambda) \, d\lambda
            = \int_a^b s_\gamma(\lambda) \, d\lambda
            = L_{[a,b]}[\gamma].
        \]</span>  In the orientation reversing case, <span class="math inline">\(|\textrm{\runic ᚱ}'| = -\textrm{\runic ᚱ}'\)</span>, and the extra sign compensates the exchange of the integration limits,  <span class="math display">\[
            L_{[\tilde{a}, \tilde{b}]}[\delta]
            = -\int_{\tilde{a}}^{\tilde{b}} s_\gamma\big( \textrm{\runic ᚱ}(\tilde{\lambda}) \big) \, \textrm{\runic ᚱ}'(\tilde{\lambda}) \, d\tilde{\lambda}
            = -\int_{b}^{a} s_\gamma(\lambda) \, d\lambda
            = \int_a^b s_\gamma(\lambda) \, d\lambda
            = L_{[a,b]}[\gamma]. \qquad \square
        \]</span></p></li>
</ul>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Remarks.</strong></p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>The speed itself is <em>not</em> invariant: <span class="math inline">\(s_\delta = |\textrm{\runic ᚱ}'| \, (s_\gamma \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}) \neq s_\gamma \circ \textrm{\runic ᚱ}\)</span> in general. Only its integral is, because the factor <span class="math inline">\(|\textrm{\runic ᚱ}'|\)</span> is exactly the Jacobian of the change of integration variable. This is why the speed is a property of the parametrized curve, while the length is a property of the path it traces.</p></li>
<li><p>The square root in the definition of <span class="math inline">\(s_\gamma\)</span> is what produces <span class="math inline">\(|\textrm{\runic ᚱ}'|\)</span> rather than <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᚱ}'\)</span>, making the length also independent of the direction in which the path is traversed.</p></li>
</ul>
